sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Pike Walk, also known as Inchworm or Walkout, is a dynamic bodyweight movement that builds core strength, hamstring flexibility, and shoulder stability in one fluid pattern.

By alternating between a hinged toe-touch position and a full plank, the Pike Walk simultaneously stretches the posterior chain while challenging the core and upper body.

It is commonly used as a dynamic warm-up, mobility drill, and low-impact conditioning exercise in bodyweight training, yoga-flow-style workouts, and athletic preparation routines.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Strengthens the core through the plank phase
- Improves hamstring and calf flexibility
- Enhances shoulder stability and scapular control
- Builds full-body coordination
- Excellent dynamic warm-up for lower and upper body
- Improves mobility in the posterior chain
- Strengthens the wrists and forearms
- No equipment required
- Scales easily for all fitness levels
- Low impact on joints
- Develops movement quality and body awareness

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Core (Rectus Abdominis, Obliques), Shoulders, Hamstrings

Secondary: Chest, Triceps, Calves, Hip Flexors, Lower Back, Wrists

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
2. Arms relaxed at your sides.
3. Chest up, shoulders back, core engaged.
4. Eyes focused forward.
5. Clear floor space in front of you for walking out to plank.
6. Ensure a non-slip surface - barefoot or supportive footwear.
7. Breathe steadily in preparation.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Hinge at the hips and bend forward, reaching your hands to the ground in front of your feet.
2. Keep your legs as straight as possible - slight knee bend is acceptable if hamstrings are tight.
3. Place both hands flat on the floor.
4. Begin walking your hands forward one at a time, keeping your legs stationary.
5. Continue walking forward until you reach a full high plank position.
6. Hold the plank briefly - straight line from head to heels, core braced.
7. Walk your feet forward one step at a time towards your hands, keeping your legs straight.
8. Continue until you return to the hinged toe-touch position.
9. Stand tall and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Bending the knees excessively during the walk-out or walk-in
- Sagging hips in the plank position
- Piking hips too high during the plank phase
- Rushing the movement instead of controlled walking steps
- Rounding the back when hinging forward
- Holding breath through the movement
- Collapsing the shoulders or shrugging towards the ears
- Not fully extending to a proper plank position
- Moving the feet instead of walking the hands out (and vice versa)
- Letting the lower back overarch in the plank

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- No equipment required
- Non-slip flat surface or yoga mat
- Barefoot or supportive athletic footwear
- Optional: Yoga mat for wrist and knee cushioning
- Optional: Push-up handles to reduce wrist strain
- Optional: Timer for set-based or interval work

sections.heading: Programming Options
sections.content:
1. Warm-Up: 5-8 slow reps before a workout.
2. Beginner: 2-3 sets of 5 reps.
3. Intermediate: 3-4 sets of 8-10 reps.
4. Advanced: 3-4 sets of 12-15 reps.
5. Flow Work: Combine with push-ups or shoulder taps at the plank.
6. Mobility Circuit: Include with other dynamic stretches.
7. Rest: 30-60 seconds between sets.
8. Tempo: Slow and controlled for maximum mobility and control benefit.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Posture: Tall and upright at the start of each rep.
2. Hinge: From the hips, not the lower back.
3. Legs: As straight as possible - slight knee bend acceptable.
4. Hands: Shoulder-width apart on the floor.
5. Plank: Straight line from head to heels - no sagging or piking.
6. Core: Braced throughout the movement.
7. Shoulders: Pulled away from the ears, engaged.
8. Feet: Small, controlled steps during the walk-in phase.
9. Breathing: Exhale on effort, inhale during the transitions.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Inchworm: Often used interchangeably with Pike Walk
- Walkout to Push-Up: Adds a push-up at the plank position
- Downward Dog to Plank: Yoga-inspired mobility alternative
- Bear Crawl: Ground-based full-body mobility
- World's Greatest Stretch: Dynamic multi-muscle stretch
- Cat-Cow: Spinal mobility alternative
- Plank Shoulder Taps: Static plank with added core challenge

sections.heading: Pike Walk Variations
sections.content:
Standard Pike Walk: Walk out and walk back without extras
Pike Walk to Push-Up: Add a push-up at the plank position
Pike Walk to Plank Hold: Hold the plank for 5-10 seconds each rep
Pike Walk with Shoulder Tap: Alternate shoulder taps at the plank
Pike Walk with Knee Drive: Drive a knee towards chest at the plank
Fast Pike Walk: Increased pace for cardio component
One-Arm Pike Walk: Walk out on a single arm at a time (advanced)
Weighted Pike Walk: Wearing a weighted vest for added resistance

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Tight Hamstrings: Allow a slight knee bend during the hinge and walk-in
Wrist Pain: Use push-up handles or fists to maintain neutral wrist position
Shoulder Issues: Reduce the depth of the plank or skip the plank hold
Lower Back Pain: Focus on strong core bracing and avoid hyperextension
Balance Concerns: Perform against a raised surface (hands on a bench)
Beginner: Bend the knees as needed to reach the floor comfortably
Returning from Injury: Keep movements small and controlled - build range gradually
Limited Floor Space: Perform in place by moving slower and smaller
